paragraphs: Training on a small subset is useful only if that subset preserves what matters about the full dataset. This paper studies selection when data embeddings share a low-dimensional algebraic structure. Such structure can be captured by low-rank approximation even when grouping examples into clusters is less suitable.

The proposed framework combines low-rank approximation with residual-based sampling. It treats examples as rows of an embedding matrix and constructs a weighted subset intended to preserve average loss. Under stated regularity conditions on the embeddings, roughly k plus 1/ε² examples, ignoring logarithmic factors, provide a relative-error approximation with an additional εΦ_k error term. Here, Φ_k measures how much structure the best rank-k approximation leaves unexplained.

The guarantee therefore connects selection quality to how well low-rank structure represents the embeddings; it is conditional on the regularity assumptions and includes an additive error. Experiments on several real-world datasets report improvements over uniform sampling and clustering-based sensitivity sampling, supporting algebraic structure as a useful basis for data selection.
icml-2026-active-learning-with-low-rank-.tldr: A low-rank data selection method builds small weighted subsets with conditional loss-preservation guarantees and reported improvements over sampling and clustering alternatives.

paragraphs: Resettable streams allow a key’s value to increase or return to zero, supporting settings such as resource monitoring with deletions and machine unlearning. The challenge is to summarize these streams using little memory while remaining accurate when an adversary adapts its updates to previous outputs. The paper shows that existing sketches are vulnerable even with memory polynomial in stream length.

The authors construct adaptively robust sketches whose space usage grows only polylogarithmically with stream length. Their framework covers statistics including cardinality, sum, L_p moments for p between zero and one, and Bernstein statistics. They use dedicated single-stream designs to avoid impossibility results affecting linear and composable sketches.

Differential privacy protects the sketches’ internal randomness through the Binary Tree Mechanism for continual observation. This is significant because standard privacy-based robustification still requires polynomial space in this setting. The resulting framework obtains prefix-max error guarantees alongside its compact memory requirement, showing that robustness becomes achievable through a different sketch design and a mechanism tailored to repeated observation.
icml-2026-adaptively-robust-resettable-s.tldr: Dedicated sketches use differential privacy to support compact, adaptively robust summaries of streams whose values can increase or reset.

paragraphs: A common way to adapt a pretrained vision model cheaply is to freeze it and train a small prediction head. Standard linear probing typically uses its final-layer representation. This paper argues that this leaves useful information unused because different layers retain different kinds of task-relevant evidence.

Attentive layer fusion, or ALF, learns how to combine representations from across a Vision Transformer’s layers. Its attention mechanism identifies which layers matter for the target task, bringing together structural information from lower levels and more abstract semantic information from higher levels. The adaptation process can therefore draw on the network’s hierarchy instead of depending entirely on its final representation.

Across 20 datasets and multiple pretrained foundation models, ALF produces consistent, substantial improvements over standard linear probes. Attention heatmaps suggest that intermediate layers are especially valuable when the downstream task differs from the pretraining domain. These findings support task-aware layer selection as an effective way to make probing-based adaptation use more of what a pretrained model already represents.
icml-2026-attentive-multi-layer-fusion-f.tldr: ALF improves frozen Vision Transformer adaptation by learning which layers to combine for each downstream task.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents must adapt to change without losing useful knowledge. Many studies examine abrupt changes, but gradual drift may place different demands on this balance. The authors modify 3D Miniworld and MuJoCo environments to study continual change and compare approaches that emphasize preserving knowledge with those that emphasize rapid adaptation.

In these environments, stability-oriented methods such as synaptic consolidation outperform plasticity-oriented methods such as parameter resetting. Motivated by this result, the paper investigates consolidating successor features rather than Q-values. Successor features provide predictive representations, making them a possible place to preserve useful structure while the environment evolves.

Consolidating successor features improves performance across both environments, and stabilization across multiple timescales works best. Those timescales capture complementary aspects of gradual change, allowing different parts of the predictive representation to retain information over different durations. The results suggest that gradual drift can make stability especially important; they support multi-timescale consolidation in the tested continual-change settings rather than establishing that stability always dominates adaptation.
icml-2026-balancing-plasticity-and-stabi.tldr: Experiments with gradually changing environments favor stabilizing successor features across multiple timescales to balance retention and adaptation.

paragraphs: Counterfactual credit attribution formalizes the goal of crediting source material on which a generated output significantly depends. This paper brings that condition to autoregressive generation, focusing on credit assigned to a dataset available at deployment time, such as a retrieval database. It studies whether two natural construction strategies can provide the required attribution.

The first strategy imposes the condition on the next-token predictor. The authors show that this does not guarantee the condition for the complete generated output. Even if individual prediction steps satisfy the attribution requirement, their autoregressive composition need not do so. This differs from the composition behavior of differential privacy, of which the attribution condition is a relaxation.

The second strategy adds attribution to an existing model through black-box access. For this retrofitting approach, the required number of queries grows exponentially with output length. Together, the results identify barriers to these two routes: local next-token guarantees do not automatically extend to full outputs, and black-box retrofitting can be prohibitively query-intensive.
icml-2026-barriers-to-counterfactual-cre.tldr: Counterfactual attribution does not automatically compose across generated tokens, and black-box retrofitting requires exponentially many queries in output length.

paragraphs: Mixed-integer optimization solvers can find an optimal solution well before they finish proving that no better solution exists. That gap between finding and certifying a solution creates an opportunity to save computation. This paper learns when to stop a solver on recurring problems drawn from a distribution of similar instances.

A neural network examines the solver’s state and estimates the true optimality gap: how far the current solution is from the best possible one. Conformal prediction then calibrates the stopping threshold. This calibration turns a learned estimate into a stopping rule with a probabilistic guarantee on solution quality, allowing termination before a full optimality proof.

Across six problem families from Distributional MIPLIB, the method reduces solve time by more than 60%. Its stated guarantee is a 0.1%-optimal solution with 95% probability for new instances from the same distribution. That distributional condition matters: the result supports faster solving with calibrated quality assurance when future instances follow the problem distribution used by the method.
icml-2026-conformal-prediction-for-early.tldr: A conformally calibrated stopping rule cuts reported solve time by over 60% while guaranteeing 0.1%-optimal solutions with 95% probability on same-distribution instances.

paragraphs: Matching distributions across different domains can require preserving both feature correspondence and relationships within each domain. Convex Distance Operator Transport, or CDOT, addresses these goals in a convex optimization framework. Its central move is to align aggregated distance structures using distance and conditional expectation operators.

This operator-based regularization is designed to improve robustness to local geometric variation. The authors prove that the resulting discrepancy is a pseudometric on attributed compact metric-measure spaces, giving it a formal interpretation as a distance-like comparison. They also introduce a dispersion gap to explain the geometric source of non-convexity in Gromov–Wasserstein transport relative to CDOT.

For finite samples, the paper separates its risk bound into optimization error and statistical error. It establishes risk consistency under a globally convergent Frank–Wolfe algorithm, connecting the formulation to an optimization procedure with theoretical support. Experiments on synthetic point clouds, brain connectomes, and graph classification report better performance than existing methods, with stable practical behavior. The contribution combines geometric alignment, convex optimization, and statistical analysis in one framework.
icml-2026-convex-distance-operator-trans.tldr: CDOT uses operator-based distance alignment to preserve features and geometry within a convex transport framework with optimization and statistical guarantees.

paragraphs: Post-training alignment does not remove the need for moderation when language models are deployed. The paper addresses the tension between moderation quality, computational cost, and customization. Its proposed Multi-Layer Prototype Moderator, or MLPM, operates on inputs and uses representations already present inside a language model.

MLPM draws on prototypes of intermediate representations across several layers. These prototypes provide reference patterns for moderation, allowing the method to use information from multiple stages of the model’s processing. The design aims to keep additional generation overhead negligible while remaining customizable to user requirements and applicable across models.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on diverse moderation benchmarks and strong scalability across model families and sizes. They also evaluate integration into end-to-end moderation pipelines, finding that combining MLPM with output moderation further improves response safety. The findings support multi-layer internal representations as a practical resource for efficient input screening, with input and output moderation making complementary contributions to the evaluated safety pipeline.
icml-2026-efficient-llm-moderation-with-.tldr: MLPM uses prototypes from multiple internal model layers for efficient, customizable input moderation and complements output moderation.

paragraphs: Autoregressive image generation depends on a tokenizer that compresses an image into a sequence of latent representations. The generative model then learns to produce those representations. This paper revisits the training relationship between these components, which prior two-stage approaches optimize separately.

The authors introduce joint training for image reconstruction and generation. This allows the results of generation to directly supervise the tokenizer, so the representation is shaped by the task of producing images as well as reconstructing them. They also investigate using vision foundation models to improve one-dimensional tokenizers for autoregressive modeling. The key design change is therefore in how the tokenizer and generator learn together.

The resulting autoregressive model achieves a reported state-of-the-art FID of 1.48 without guidance on ImageNet generation at 256-by-256 resolution. This is an empirical result for the stated setting. It supports the value of connecting representation learning to generation during training, rather than treating tokenizer quality and generative modeling as entirely separate optimization problems.
icml-2026-end-to-end-autoregressive-imag.tldr: Jointly training an image tokenizer and autoregressive generator enables generation feedback to shape the representation and yields a reported unguided FID of 1.48.

paragraphs: Language models can turn goals and environmental constraints into executable control programs for embodied agents. However, repeatedly processing long prompts slows generation, while generating every program afresh can introduce API errors, missing safety checks, or unstable control logic. FCGraft addresses both issues by reusing validated functions and their cached model computations.

Its library stores function-level code skeletons alongside Transformer key–value caches associated with their prompts. For a new task, the system retrieves relevant functions and combines their cached segments through stitching. It then uses patching to adapt only the code regions needed for the task’s parameters and constraints, limiting additional decoding.

This design links computational reuse to reuse of validated program structure. Avoiding redundant prompt processing reduces latency, while preserving established control structures improves robustness in the reported evaluation. Compared with RAGCache, the abstract reports an 18.31% higher task success rate and 2.3-times faster policy synthesis. The findings support function-level reuse as a way to improve both generation speed and the reliability of embodied code policies.
icml-2026-functional-cache-grafting-robu.tldr: FCGraft combines validated function skeletons and cached Transformer computations to synthesize embodied control code faster and more reliably.

paragraphs: Vision representations are often judged by how well their embeddings are distributed globally. This paper asks whether such geometry also reveals a model’s ability to represent how visual elements are composed. Recognizing which elements are present and correctly binding them into a composite structure are different capabilities.

Across 21 vision encoders, standard geometric statistics have near-zero correlation with compositional binding. Functional sensitivity, measured using the input-output Jacobian, tracks this capability more reliably. The Jacobian describes how the representation changes as the input changes, providing a view of the model’s local behavior that a global summary of embedding positions can miss.

The authors also give an analytic explanation based on training objectives. Existing losses explicitly constrain embedding geometry while leaving the local input-output mapping unconstrained, allowing the two forms of assessment to diverge. The findings suggest that global geometry provides a partial picture of representation quality. Functional sensitivity offers a complementary measurement for assessing whether representations capture relationships among elements, beyond recording their presence.
icml-2026-global-geometry-is-not-enough-.tldr: Across 21 vision encoders, local input-output sensitivity tracks compositional binding while standard global embedding geometry metrics show near-zero correlation.

paragraphs: Estimating a discrete probability distribution means assigning probabilities to its possible outcomes from observations. This paper measures estimation error using the infinity norm, which focuses on the largest absolute error for any single outcome. It develops improved bounds for that criterion, making the worst individual probability estimate central to the analysis.

The results cover both minimax bounds in expectation and high-probability tail bounds. These address different questions: how large the expected error can be in the hardest case, and how likely an unusually large error is. The authors also obtain a fully empirical version of the tightest risk bound in the prior work they discuss, bringing that bound into a form based on observed data.

Another contribution identifies the form of a worst-case extremal distribution, clarifying what makes distribution estimation difficult under this error measure. The paper reports encouraging empirical results alongside the theory. Its stated advances concern sharper error guarantees, an empirical formulation of a risk bound, and a characterization of a hardest-case distribution.
icml-2026-improved-distribution-estimati.tldr: The paper sharpens infinity-norm distribution estimation bounds, provides an empirical risk bound, and identifies the form of a worst-case distribution.

paragraphs: A robot can receive a clear goal and still struggle to learn why an attempt failed. LAGEA investigates whether structured language feedback can help diagnose mistakes and guide subsequent learning. It uses a vision-language model to produce concise reflections about each attempt, following a constrained schema.

The framework connects those reflections to decisive moments in the robot’s trajectory and aligns the feedback with visual states in a shared representation. It then converts goal progress and agreement with the feedback into bounded rewards at individual steps. An adaptive, failure-aware coefficient controls their influence, providing stronger guidance early in exploration and reducing it as competence increases.

On Meta-World MT10 and Robotic Fetch, the authors report average success improvements over state-of-the-art methods of 9.0% for random goals, 5.3% for fixed goals, and 17% for fetch tasks, along with faster convergence. These results support the idea that language can serve as a useful learning signal when its feedback is structured and connected to the timing of actions and outcomes.
icml-2026-lagea-language-guided-embodied.tldr: LAGEA turns structured, temporally grounded language reflections into adaptive learning rewards that improve reported robotic manipulation success.

paragraphs: Online minimization requires making decisions as a problem unfolds, without having all future information available. This paper studies how learned predictions can improve algorithms for metrical task systems and laminar set cover. Its central choice is to predict an optimal solution of the dual linear program rather than the original, or primal, optimization problem.

The motivation is stability across related instances. An optimal primal solution may change sharply after a small change to the problem, making it a difficult prediction target. The authors argue that the corresponding dual solutions are substantially more stable, ensuring the existence of good, learnable predictions for families of similar instances.

Using these dual predictions, the paper develops algorithms with improved theoretical guarantees for both problem classes. Experiments on the k-server and parking permit problems complement the theory. The authors position the work as, to their knowledge, the first demonstration of effective dual predictions for online minimization, extending an approach previously used in offline optimization and online maximization.
icml-2026-learning-augmented-online-mini.tldr: Predicting more stable dual solutions improves theoretical guarantees for online algorithms in metrical task systems and laminar set cover.

paragraphs: Long prompts can supply many worked examples, but their usefulness for reasoning may depend on more than quantity. This paper studies many-shot chain-of-thought in-context learning across reasoning and non-reasoning tasks, using both reasoning-oriented and other language models. It examines how demonstrations function when a model must follow and apply reasoning.

The authors interpret their findings as evidence for in-context test-time learning rather than simply more extensive pattern matching. They suggest that demonstrations should be understandable to the target model and arranged in a smooth conceptual progression. Under this view, a long context can act as a curriculum whose sequence helps organize the material.

These principles motivate Curvilinear Demonstration Selection, a simple ordering method. On a math task with 64 demonstrations, it produces a gain of up to 5.42 percentage points. The reported improvement supports paying attention to demonstration order as well as content, while the broader curriculum interpretation provides a proposed explanation for the distinctive behavior observed in many-shot reasoning.
icml-2026-many-shot-cot-icl-making-in-co.tldr: Ordering understandable reasoning demonstrations into a conceptual progression yields up to a 5.42-percentage-point gain on a math task with 64 examples.

paragraphs: Tracking an entity requires maintaining a coherent account of its state as new information arrives. MET-Bench tests this ability when updates come through both text and images. The benchmark spans three domains and extends entity-tracking evaluation beyond purely textual tasks to examine how vision-language models integrate information across modalities.

The authors find a substantial performance gap between text-based and image-based tracking. Their empirical analysis attributes this gap primarily to visual reasoning deficits rather than perception. Explicit text-based reasoning strategies improve performance, but difficulties remain, especially when models must maintain entity states over long sequences of multimodal updates.

The paper also applies reinforcement learning to open-source vision-language models. Training brings substantial improvements within the input modality used, but those gains do not transfer robustly across modalities. This distinguishes improvement on a particular presentation format from a broadly transferable tracking capability. The results point to multimodal representations and reasoning as important targets for improving consistent state tracking across textual and visual information.
icml-2026-met-bench-multimodal-entity-tr.tldr: MET-Bench reveals weaknesses in visual entity-state reasoning and finds that reinforcement learning gains do not transfer robustly across input modalities.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning can use a learned model to imagine trajectories and estimate the value of actions. However, repeatedly feeding predicted states back into that model can compound errors. Geometric horizon models reduce this repeated prediction by directly modeling a discounted future, but accurately representing distant states remains difficult.

Universal horizon models generalize that approach by directly predicting future states for arbitrary horizons. This gives the learning procedure flexibility over how far ahead it asks the model to predict. The proposed value-learning method uses a winsorized horizon distribution, which caps excessively large horizons to stabilize training while retaining a range of prediction distances.

Across 100 challenging OGBench tasks, the method outperforms competitive baselines, with particular strengths on highly suboptimal datasets and tasks requiring long-horizon reasoning. These results support flexible direct future prediction as a useful approach to offline value learning. The horizon cap is an integral part of the method: it manages the difficulty of distant predictions while the model supports different look-ahead distances.
icml-2026-offline-reinforcement-learning.tldr: Universal horizon models predict future states at flexible horizons, with capped training horizons improving offline reinforcement learning across 100 OGBench tasks.

paragraphs: Concept Bottleneck Models make predictions through concepts intended to be understandable to people. However, assigning a human-readable concept name does not establish that the model has learned the meaning a person intended. This paper addresses that verification problem by attaching visible evidence to the concepts used in prediction.

Prototype-Grounded Concept Models represent concepts through learned visual prototypes: image parts that explicitly support a concept. A person can inspect those parts to assess what the model associates with the concept. The same grounding supports targeted intervention at the prototype level, giving people a way to correct a specific semantic misalignment.

The authors report predictive performance similar to state-of-the-art Concept Bottleneck Models, alongside substantial improvements in transparency, interpretability, and the ability to intervene. The contribution is therefore a more inspectable connection between concept names and learned visual evidence. It supports checking and correcting the meaning of a model’s concepts while retaining comparable predictive performance in the reported empirical evaluation.
icml-2026-prototype-grounded-concept-mod.tldr: Visual prototypes make learned concepts inspectable and correctable while preserving predictive performance comparable to leading concept bottleneck models.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a hypothesis class admits a learner whose risk converges to zero for every realizable data distribution. Realizability means the class contains a predictor with zero risk for that distribution. The setting allows general metric losses, including unbounded ones, extending the question beyond classification and real-valued regression.

The authors provide necessary and sufficient conditions for a distribution-free learning rule with almost-sure convergence to the best-in-class risk. This is a characterization of when such learning is possible, rather than only a sufficient recipe for selected classes. It resolves the realizable case of the open problem discussed in the abstract.

The characterization uses a combinatorial obstruction based on an infinite Littlestone-type tree with non-decreasing scale parameters that grow without bound. This extends the tree structure used in earlier classification analyses to metric losses. The result connects the possibility of consistent learning to a structural property of the hypothesis class, with the guarantee applying specifically to realizable data-generating distributions.
icml-2026-realizable-bayes-consistency-f.tldr: The paper characterizes exactly when realizable learning with general metric losses admits distribution-free, almost-sure convergence to zero risk.

paragraphs: Medical image segmentation needs both broad image context and sensitivity to local shapes. S2M-Net addresses this with a 4.7-million-parameter architecture that combines frequency-domain processing and spatial gating. Its spectral-spatial mixing preserves a global receptive field while avoiding the attention-map computation that grows quadratically with image area.

The design exploits spectral concentration: the abstract reports that 32 low-frequency components capture more than 93% of the energy in the stated setting. A separate adaptive loss adjusts five objectives using each sample’s tubularity, compactness, irregularity, and scale. This lets training respond to geometric differences among structures instead of using the same objective balance for every sample.

Across 15 datasets and eight modalities, S2M-Net achieves the best reported performance on 14 datasets, with statistically significant gains on seven challenging tasks. On EndoVis17, it reaches 83.43% Dice versus 74.29% for UMamba while using 4.7 million rather than 60 million parameters. The results support combining efficient global processing with shape-aware training for the evaluated segmentation problems.
icml-2026-s2m-net-spectral-spatial-mixin.tldr: S2M-Net combines efficient spectral-spatial processing with shape-adaptive training, achieving the best reported segmentation performance on 14 of 15 datasets.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation identifies individual objects in scenes using flexible language descriptions. Existing approaches can be slow or depend on external proposals for candidate object regions. SpaCeFormer predicts instance masks directly from learned queries, aiming to remove that proposal dependency while accelerating scene processing.

The model combines spatial window attention with Morton-curve serialization, which arranges scene information to preserve spatial coherence. Its decoder adds rotary positional encoding. The authors also build SpaCeFormer-3M using multi-view mask clustering and vision-language captioning, producing 3.0 million captions over 604,000 instances from 7,400 scenes. Its reported mask recall is 54.3%, compared with 2.5% for prior single-view pipelines at the stated overlap threshold.

SpaCeFormer runs in 0.12–0.30 seconds per scene across the evaluated benchmarks. It achieves 11.1 zero-shot mAP on ScanNet200, 2.8 times the prior best proposal-free result, and reports 22.9 and 24.1 mAP on ScanNet++ and Replica. The findings combine a faster direct-prediction architecture with training data that better consolidates objects across views.
icml-2026-spaceformer-fast-proposal-free.tldr: SpaCeFormer combines direct 3D mask prediction and multi-view captioned training data to deliver fast, improved open-vocabulary instance segmentation.

paragraphs: Robot poses combine translation and rotation, giving them geometric constraints that arbitrary flat vectors do not respect. This paper argues that representing poses as twelve-dimensional Euclidean vectors in diffusion-based vision-language-action policies can violate rotation constraints, break consistency under coordinate changes, and produce trajectories with excessive kinematic cost.

Lie Diffuser Actor operates directly on SE(3), the space of rigid-body poses. It adds noise through left-invariant stochastic dynamics, predicts scores in tangent space, and maps samples back through the exponential map. The formulation eliminates drift off the pose manifold by construction and, according to the paper, guarantees coordinate-frame equivariance and geodesic optimality.

On the CALVIN ABC-to-D setting, average task length increases from 3.27 to 3.51, a 7.3% improvement. Real-robot evaluation also finds that the method outperforms the baseline on a majority of tasks. These results provide empirical support for respecting pose geometry inside the diffusion process, alongside the formulation’s stated geometric guarantees; the real-robot finding does not claim improvement on every task.
icml-2026-the-lie-we-tell-correcting-the.tldr: Lie Diffuser Actor respects rigid-pose geometry during diffusion, providing stated geometric guarantees and improving evaluated robot manipulation performance.

paragraphs: Transformers are usually trained to model statistical patterns, but their components may also execute exact algorithms. This paper constructs a transformer from first principles to implement Lloyd’s algorithm for k-means clustering. The construction uses familiar components: attention, residual connections, and feed-forward blocks.

The authors prove exact implementation and demonstrate it empirically. They then train the same base architecture on clustering tasks, obtaining a generalizable learned clustering algorithm that surpasses Lloyd’s algorithm in clustering quality in their experiments. This separates two contributions: a designed circuit that performs a known routine exactly, and a trainable architecture that can develop a different routine with better observed results.

Interpretable architectural changes, including the addition of layer normalization, produce variants such as soft, spherical, and trimmed k-means. These connections make architectural choices meaningful in algorithmic terms rather than treating them only as modeling adjustments. The work shows that transformer mechanisms can both instantiate an exact clustering computation and provide a structured starting point for learning alternative clustering behavior.
icml-2026-transformer-circuits-can-reali.tldr: A constructed transformer exactly implements Lloyd’s k-means algorithm, while training and interpretable architectural changes yield other effective clustering routines.

paragraphs: An ensemble combines multiple models, but evaluating every model for every input can be expensive. LazyStack checks after each model whether the accumulated evidence supports a confident exit. When more evidence is needed, trained meta-learners combine predictions from additional models, joining early-exit routing with learned aggregation.

The method uses the observation that most inputs follow only three to eight execution trajectories. It trains aggregators for these common paths, reducing the training problem from exponential to linear. It also treats trajectory selection as a Markov decision process and uses value iteration to compute an optimal routing policy within that formulation.

The resulting order can differ from simply running the cheapest model first. On intrusion detection, a moderately expensive first model performs better because its confidence enables earlier overall exits. Across vision, text, tabular, and language-model tasks, LazyStack reports speedups of up to 38 times while retaining at least 97% of complete-ensemble accuracy. The findings emphasize total decision cost rather than the cost of an individual model.
icml-2026-unifying-stacking-and-cascadin.tldr: LazyStack learns how to combine and route ensemble models, reporting up to 38-fold speedups with at least 97% accuracy retention.

paragraphs: Decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning allows agents to share value estimates to accelerate learning. However, agents may have performed different numbers of online updates, leaving their estimates with unequal uncertainty. The paper studies how averaging those estimates can undo learning progress, a phenomenon it calls learning rollback.

The authors formally characterize rollback under heterogeneous update depths and propose adaptive global consensus for Q-value aggregation in policy evaluation. The mechanism changes aggregation weights according to agents’ uncertainty. This makes the combination responsive to differences in the estimates instead of treating a conventional convex average as an adequate default throughout learning.

The paper establishes theoretical guarantees for accelerated convergence and bounded learning variance, accompanied by empirical validation. These results support accounting for uncertainty when agents exchange value information during online learning. The stated scope is decentralized policy evaluation: the contribution concerns how shared Q-value estimates are combined and how that combination affects convergence and variability, rather than a general guarantee of globally optimal policies for every multi-agent task.
icml-2026-value-aggregation-with-uncerta.tldr: Uncertainty-aware Q-value aggregation addresses learning rollback and provides convergence and variance guarantees for decentralized multi-agent policy evaluation.
